1	# Releasing Hey Reachy
2	
3	Signed artifacts are produced locally; CI only publishes the GitHub release with
4	generated notes. Credentials never enter the repository or CI.
5	
6	## One-time setup
7	
8	1. **App Store Connect API key** — App Store Connect → Users and Access →
9	   Integrations → App Store Connect API → Team Keys, role **App Manager**.
10	   Download the `.p8` once and write the credentials file:
11	
12	   ```bash
13	   mkdir -p ~/.config/reachy-mini
14	   cat > ~/.config/reachy-mini/release.env <<'CONF'
15	   REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=XXXXXXXXXX
16	   REACHY_ASC_KEY_ID=XXXXXXXXXX
17	   REACHY_ASC_ISSUER_ID=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
18	   REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH=/Users/you/.config/reachy-mini/AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8
19	   CONF
20	   ```
21	
22	2. **App IDs and the App Group** — the first signed build with
23	   `-allowProvisioningUpdates` registers the bundle ids
24	   (`com.alexey1312.ReachyMini`, `.Widget`), but the
25	   `group.com.alexey1312.ReachyMini` capability must be added by hand in
26	   Xcode's Signing & Capabilities, once per App ID (app and widget separately,
27	   iOS and macOS separately). `xcodebuild` cannot create it.
28	
29	3. **App Store Connect app record** — My Apps → New App:
30	   - Name: **Hey Reachy**; if taken, fall back to “Hey Reachy — robot remote”.
31	   - Subtitle: **Control your Reachy Mini**.
32	   - Bundle id `com.alexey1312.ReachyMini`.
33	   - The description must state it is an unofficial client for Reachy Mini by
34	     Pollen Robotics. A public TestFlight link goes through Beta App Review, so
35	     the name is checked before any App Store submission.
36	   - App Privacy: no data collected. The app talks to the robot on the local
37	     network and to Hugging Face with the user's own OAuth session; nothing is
38	     sent to the developer.
39	   - Encryption: answered in the Info.plist (`ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption`),
40	     ASC asks nothing per build.
41	
42	4. **Developer ID Application certificate** (macOS) — Xcode → Settings →
43	   Accounts → Manage Certificates → “+” → Developer ID Application.
44	
45	5. **macOS ships through both channels**, so the Mac App Store one needs its own
46	   signing assets besides the Developer ID certificate: Apple Distribution and
47	   Mac Installer Distribution. `-allowProvisioningUpdates` creates them through
48	   the Xcode account the same way it does for iOS. The app record already
49	   carries a macOS platform beside the iOS one — `mise run asc -- versions list
50	   --app 6799644194` shows both — so nothing has to be created in App Store
51	   Connect. What is not automatic is the App Group: step 2 registers it per App
52	   ID, and the macOS App ID is a separate one from the iOS App ID.
53	
54	## Each release
55	
56	1. Bump `MARKETING_VERSION` in `Apps/Project.swift` (bare semver, e.g. `0.2.0`)
57	   and land it on `main`. Build numbers are the commit count — nothing to bump.
58	2. Tag and push; the tag triggers the GitHub release with git-cliff notes:
59	
60	   ```bash
61	   git tag 0.2.0 && git push origin 0.2.0
62	   ```
63	
64	3. Produce and ship the artifacts:
65	
66	   ```bash
67	   mise run release:ios     # archive → TestFlight
68	   mise run release:macos   # archive → both macOS channels (see below)
69	   gh release upload 0.2.0 Apps/DerivedData/Export/macOS/HeyReachy-0.2.0.zip
70	   ```
71	
72	`release:macos` archives once and exports that archive twice, because
73	`-exportArchive` re-signs per method — the two artifacts are the same build:
74	
75	| Channel        | Method            | Artifact                           | Ends up in              |
76	| -------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
77	| `developer-id` | notarize → staple | `Export/macOS/HeyReachy-<ver>.zip` | GitHub release, by hand |
78	| `appstore`     | upload            | `.pkg` (not kept)                  | TestFlight for macOS    |
79	
80	Developer ID runs first on purpose: it is the artifact that always ships, and a
81	failed App Store upload should not also cost you the zip. Pick one channel with
82	`--channel appstore` or `--channel developer-id`.
83	
84	Both archive commands compile with the Xcode compilation cache off
85	(`COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING=NO`) and then run
86	`Scripts/check-appintents-metadata.sh` against the archive before anything is
87	exported or uploaded. The intents live in a static SPM library, so the
88	Shortcuts app only ever sees what `appintentsmetadataprocessor` extracted into
89	`Metadata.appintents` — and extraction failing is a warning, never a build
90	error. TestFlight 0.1.1 shipped exactly that way: green archive, no actions in
91	the Shortcuts app. The check names every missing action instead; if it fails,
92	the fix is in the build, not in App Store Connect.
93	
94	Dry runs: `mise run release:ios -- --no-upload` exports an `.ipa` without
95	uploading; `mise run release:macos -- --no-notarize` stops the Developer ID
96	channel after the signed export, and `--no-upload` makes the App Store channel
97	leave a `.pkg` in `Export/macOS/AppStore` instead of uploading it. Each flag
98	belongs to one channel and is ignored by the other.
99	
100	## The public beta
101	
102	`https://testflight.apple.com/join/CGjefT9a` — the **Public Beta** group,
103	`c48f6abb-c178-40a2-8747-b6513add766e`, capped at 500 testers. The link is in
104	the README; raising the cap is one `groups edit --public-link-limit`, lowering
105	it below the people who already joined is not.
106	
107	Uploading is not distributing. An upload reaches the internal group by itself,
108	because `Internal` carries `hasAccessToAllBuilds`; the public group has to be
109	attached per build, per platform, and each one is its own Beta App Review:
110	
111	```bash
112	mise run asc -- builds add-groups --app 6799644194 --latest --platform IOS \
113	  --group c48f6abb-c178-40a2-8747-b6513add766e --submit --confirm
114	mise run asc -- builds add-groups --app 6799644194 --latest --platform MAC_OS \
115	  --group c48f6abb-c178-40a2-8747-b6513add766e --submit --confirm
116	mise run asc -- testflight review submissions list --build-id "<id>"
117	```
118	
119	What review reads lives at the app level, not the build level, so it is written
120	once and stays: the tester-facing text in `testflight app-localizations`
121	(description, feedback email, marketing URL, and the privacy policy at
122	`docs/privacy.md` — which has to resolve on `main`, or review fails on a 404),
123	and the reviewer-facing contact and notes in `testflight review edit`. The notes
124	carry the thing no reviewer can guess — that the app needs a robot nobody at
125	Apple has, that the Bluetooth sheet auto-presenting on first launch hides the
126	Local Network alert underneath it, and that Hugging Face sign-in is the one path
127	that completes without hardware. Beta App Review has no demo account to give,
128	because the app has no accounts.
129	
130	Testers see the same What to Test note per build:
131	
132	```bash
133	mise run asc -- builds test-notes create --build-id "<id>" \
134	  --locale en-US --whats-new "..."
135	```
136	
137	## Querying App Store Connect
138	
139	`mise run asc` is the App Store Connect CLI with the same key already loaded —
140	`Scripts/asc.sh` maps the `REACHY_ASC_*` values onto the `ASC_*` names the tool
141	reads, so nothing is stored twice and no keychain profile exists to drift.
142	Everything after `--` goes to `asc`:
143	
144	```bash
145	mise run asc -- apps list
146	mise run asc -- builds list --app 6799644194   # did the TestFlight upload land?
147	mise run asc -- testflight beta-groups list --app 6799644194
148	```
149	
150	`asc` resolves a stored profile before the environment, so an `asc auth login`
151	run by hand silently outranks this wrapper — `mise run asc -- auth status`
152	prints which of the two is answering. The key is App Manager, not Admin, so the
153	same limit release-ios.sh documents applies: it can read and submit, and it
154	cannot manage provisioning profiles.
155	
156	The CLI also ships 23 agent skills (`asc install-skills`, pinned to a reviewed
157	commit) covering TestFlight, metadata, submissions and signing.
158	
159	## Xcode Cloud (optional, continuous TestFlight)
160	
161	`Apps/ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh` makes a generated project buildable on
162	Xcode Cloud: it installs the pinned tools through the committed `bin/mise`
163	bootstrap, generates the workspace, and stamps `CI_BUILD_NUMBER` in as the
164	build number. Signing there is managed by Apple — no certificates leave the
165	account — and TestFlight distribution is a post-action checkbox. The setup
166	quirks (create the workflow from a local Xcode, start the build counter above
167	the last local upload, Git LFS is unsupported so never build the snapshot
168	scheme there) are commented at the top of the script.
169

1	#!/bin/bash
2	# Archive the iOS app (Release, signed) and upload it to TestFlight.
3	#
4	#   mise run release:ios              # archive → upload to App Store Connect
5	#   mise run release:ios -- --no-upload   # archive → export an .ipa locally
6	#
7	# Signing and uploading go through the Xcode account, not the App Store Connect
8	# API key — see release-env.sh for the measurement behind that.
9	#
10	# The build number is the commit count: monotonic, reproducible, and never
11	# stored in the repository — so releasing does not require a version-bump
12	# commit for anything but MARKETING_VERSION.
13	set -euo pipefail
14	
15	# shellcheck source=Scripts/release-env.sh
16	. "$(dirname "$0")/release-env.sh"
17	
18	upload=true
19	require_development_team
20	while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
21	  case "$1" in
22	  --no-upload) upload=false ;;
23	  *)
24	    echo "usage: release-ios.sh [--no-upload]" >&2
25	    exit 2
26	    ;;
27	  esac
28	  shift
29	done
30	
31	BUILD_NUMBER="$(git rev-list --count HEAD)"
32	ARCHIVE=Apps/DerivedData/Archives/ReachyMini-iOS.xcarchive
33	
34	set -o pipefail
35	# COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING=NO: the shipping artifact gets a clean,
36	# uncached compile. The cache went on by default the day before 0.1.1 was
37	# archived, and 0.1.1 is the build that installed from TestFlight with no
38	# Shortcuts actions at all — an archive is rare enough that replayed
39	# compilations buy nothing worth that variable. The metadata check below is
40	# what proves the archive either way, before anything is uploaded.
41	xcodebuild archive \
42	  -workspace Apps/ReachyMiniApps.xcworkspace -scheme ReachyMini \
43	  -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' -configuration Release \
44	  -archivePath "$ARCHIVE" -derivedDataPath Apps/DerivedData \
45	  DEVELOPMENT_TEAM="$REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM" CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Automatic \
46	  CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION="$BUILD_NUMBER" \
47	  COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING=NO \
48	  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
49	  -skipPackagePluginValidation -skipMacroValidation \
50	  2>&1 | xcsift
51	
52	# An archive whose Metadata.appintents came out empty ships an app with no
53	# actions in the Shortcuts app, and nothing in the build reddens over it.
54	Scripts/check-appintents-metadata.sh "$ARCHIVE"
55	
56	EXPORT_OPTIONS="$(appstore_export_options "$upload")"
57	
58	xcodebuild -exportArchive \
59	  -archivePath "$ARCHIVE" \
60	  -exportOptionsPlist "$EXPORT_OPTIONS" \
61	  -exportPath Apps/DerivedData/Export/iOS \
62	  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
63	  2>&1 | xcsift
64	
65	if [ "$upload" = true ]; then
66	  echo "Uploaded build $BUILD_NUMBER to App Store Connect. TestFlight shows it after processing (minutes)."
67	else
68	  # The archive was already checked, but the .ipa is what actually ships, and
69	  # -exportArchive re-signs and repacks on the way — so prove the metadata
70	  # survived the export too. Only the --no-upload path leaves an .ipa behind;
71	  # `destination: upload` hands the artifact straight to App Store Connect.
72	  IPA="$(ls Apps/DerivedData/Export/iOS/*.ipa | head -1)"
73	  UNPACKED="$(mktemp -d -t reachy-ipa-check)"
74	  ditto -x -k "$IPA" "$UNPACKED"
75	  Scripts/check-appintents-metadata.sh "$UNPACKED"/Payload/*.app
76	  echo "Exported without uploading:"
77	  ls Apps/DerivedData/Export/iOS/*.ipa
78	fi

1	#!/bin/bash
2	# Sourced by release-ios.sh, release-macos.sh and asc.sh: loads and checks the
3	# release credentials. Like the device signing team, they live outside every worktree in
4	# ~/.config/reachy-mini/, so nothing is copied when a workspace is created and
5	# nothing account-specific ever lands in the repository.
6	#
7	# Exported variables win over the file, so a CI machine can inject its own.
8	
9	RELEASE_CONFIG="${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/reachy-mini/release.env"
10	DEVICE_CONFIG="${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/reachy-mini/device.env"
11	
12	# The signing team is the same one device builds already use; read it first so
13	# release.env only has to add the App Store Connect key.
14	if [ -z "${REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM:-}" ] && [ -f "$DEVICE_CONFIG" ]; then
15	  # shellcheck disable=SC1090
16	  . "$DEVICE_CONFIG"
17	fi
18	if [ -f "$RELEASE_CONFIG" ]; then
19	  # shellcheck disable=SC1090
20	  . "$RELEASE_CONFIG"
21	fi
22	
23	# Demanded by the two scripts that archive; asc.sh sources this file for the API key
24	# alone and never signs anything, so the check cannot run on load.
25	require_development_team() {
26	  [ -n "${REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM:-}" ] && return 0
27	  cat >&2 <<EOF
28	No signing team. Write it once, the way device builds already expect:
29	
30	  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$DEVICE_CONFIG")"
31	  echo 'REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=XXXXXXXXXX' > "$DEVICE_CONFIG"
32	
33	The id is in Xcode → Settings → Accounts, next to the team that owns com.alexey1312.*.
34	EOF
35	  exit 1
36	}
37	
38	# The API key is optional, and deliberately unused for signing. xcodebuild takes
39	# `-authenticationKey*` as "do everything through cloud signing", and a key below
40	# the Admin role cannot manage profiles — the export then fails with "Cloud
41	# signing permission error" and "No profiles were found" even though the
42	# certificate is right there in the keychain. A key's role cannot be changed
43	# after it is created. Without the flags xcodebuild uses the Xcode account, which
44	# has the rights, so signing is left to it and the key is kept for the two things
45	# that only need to read and submit: notarization, and CI.
46	REACHY_HAS_ASC=""
47	if [ -n "${REACHY_ASC_KEY_ID:-}" ] && [ -n "${REACHY_ASC_ISSUER_ID:-}" ] && [ -n "${REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH:-}" ]; then
48	  if [ ! -f "$REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH" ]; then
49	    echo "REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH points at $REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH, which does not exist." >&2
50	    exit 1
51	  fi
52	  REACHY_HAS_ASC=1
53	fi
54	
55	# `destination: upload` in the shared plist is what hands the artifact to App Store
56	# Connect, and it is the only key a dry run has to change. Generating the copy beats
57	# keeping a second file, which would drift the moment either channel gains an option.
58	# Takes the value of the caller's own upload flag and echoes the plist to use.
59	appstore_export_options() {
60	  if [ "${1:-true}" = true ]; then
61	    echo Scripts/exportOptions/appstore.plist
62	    return 0
63	  fi
64	  local options
65	  options="$(mktemp -t reachy-export-options).plist"
66	  plutil -convert xml1 -o "$options" Scripts/exportOptions/appstore.plist
67	  plutil -replace destination -string export "$options"
68	  echo "$options"
69	}
70	
71	# Called by the macOS script, where notarytool has no other way in, and by asc.sh,
72	# which is nothing but the key.
73	require_asc_key() {
74	  [ -n "$REACHY_HAS_ASC" ] && return 0
75	  cat >&2 <<EOF
76	This needs an App Store Connect API key (App Store Connect → Users and Access →
77	Integrations → App Store Connect API). Write the three values once:
78	
79	  cat >> "$RELEASE_CONFIG" <<'CONF'
80	REACHY_ASC_KEY_ID=XXXXXXXXXX
81	REACHY_ASC_ISSUER_ID=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
82	REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH=$HOME/.config/reachy-mini/AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8
83	CONF
84	
85	The one-time App Store Connect setup is documented in docs/release.md.
86	EOF
87	  exit 1
88	}

name: xcode-account-signed-out
description: No Apple ID is signed into Xcode on this Mac, so exportArchive's upload leg fails; upload the exported artifact with asc instead
metadata:

As of 2026-08-11 there is no Apple ID signed into Xcode on this machine —
`defaults read com.apple.dt.Xcode` shows
`DVTDeveloperAccountManagerAppleIDLists → IDE.Identifiers.Prod = ()`, an empty
list. Signing certificates are still in the keychain, so archiving and a local
export both succeed; only the legs that need the *account* fail:

- iOS `-exportArchive` with `destination: upload` → `Failed to Use Accounts`,
  and the distribution log names the step: `IDEDistributionUploadAccountStep`,
  "Failed to find an account with App Store Connect access for team J52C3SB8K5".
- macOS App Store export → `No Accounts` plus
  `No signing certificate "Mac Installer Distribution" found`; that certificate
  does not exist on the account at all (`asc certificates list` shows only
  DEVELOPER_ID_APPLICATION, DISTRIBUTION and two DEVELOPMENT), because
  `-allowProvisioningUpdates` is what used to create it through the account.

**Why:** `Scripts/release-env.sh` deliberately withholds the ASC API key from
`xcodebuild` (an App Manager key turns the flags into cloud signing, which it is
not entitled to do), so the upload leg has no credential to fall back on.

**How to apply:** for iOS, export locally instead of uploading — copy
`Scripts/exportOptions/appstore.plist`, `plutil -replace destination -string export`,
run `-exportArchive` against the existing archive — then
`asc publish testflight --app 6799644194 --ipa "…/Hey Reachy.ipa" --group <id>
--test-notes … --locale en-US --wait --submit --confirm`, which uploads with the
same key and attaches the public group in one call. macOS App Store has no such
detour: it needs a Mac Installer Distribution certificate, so either sign back
into Xcode (Settings → Accounts) or mint the certificate through
`asc certificates create --certificate-type MAC_INSTALLER_DISTRIBUTION --generate-csr`
plus a Mac App Store profile. See [[asc-cli-wiring]], [[verify-testflight-upload]],
[[device-build-signing]].
